entries.transcript: I don't think free will requires that we could have made a different choice under exactly the same conditions. It might be enough that the decision came from our own reasoning rather than someone forcing us.
entries.title: our own reasoning
entries.summary: Free will as a decision arising from your own reasoning, rather than as the ability to have chosen otherwise.

entries.transcript: Database indexes trade write performance and storage for faster reads. The database has to update the index whenever the underlying data changes.
entries.title: indexes trade writes
entries.summary: An index buys read speed with write cost and storage.

entries.transcript:
Buy a new USB-C cable.
Renew GitHub token.
Book dentist for next week.
entries.title: cable, token, dentist

entries.transcript: Hash table lookup is O(1) on average, which is the guarantee a database index leans on, but that doesn't mean every lookup literally takes the same amount of time. It means the expected work stays roughly constant as the table grows, assuming a reasonable hash function and resizing strategy.
entries.title: O(1) is an average
entries.summary: Constant-time lookup describes expected work as the table grows, not a fixed cost per lookup.

entries.transcript: I think people are too quick to call software overengineered just because it has more components. Sometimes adding complexity to the implementation makes the overall system easier to reason about.
entries.title: too quick to say overengineered
entries.summary: Component count is a poor test of overengineering; more parts can make a system easier to reason about.

entries.transcript: The sunk cost fallacy is letting resources we've already spent influence a decision that should really depend on the costs and benefits from this point onward.
entries.title: sunk cost
entries.summary: Spent resources should not bear on a decision that depends on costs and benefits from here on.

entries.transcript: I'm not convinced that knowing more about a subject necessarily makes you less biased. Expertise can give you better tools for noticing your own assumptions, but it can also give you much better ways of defending them.
entries.title: expertise defends assumptions
entries.summary: Expertise supplies better tools for noticing assumptions and better tools for defending them.

entries.transcript:
Things to look into:
- Why the SQLite database handles concurrency the way it does
- Read about CRDTs
- Finish the paper on causal inference
- Fix the flaky integration test
entries.title: things to look into
actionItems: Why the SQLite database handles concurrency the way it does
Finish the paper on causal inference

entries.transcript: Retries can make distributed systems less reliable because a large number of clients can retry at the same time and put even more load on a service that's already struggling.
entries.title: retries make it worse
entries.summary: Correlated retries add load to a service that is already failing.

entries.transcript: I used to think more information generally led to better decisions. I'm starting to think the opposite can happen when the information isn't organized well. At some point additional information just makes it harder to distinguish what actually matters.
entries.title: more information, worse decisions
entries.summary: Past a point, unorganised information makes it harder to tell what matters.

entries.transcript: I'm not convinced that making an AI system more capable necessarily makes it more intelligent. A model can know more, solve harder problems, and still be bad at deciding what it should actually be doing.
entries.title: capable is not intelligent
entries.summary: Capability and intelligence come apart at deciding what to do.

entries.transcript: Scaling language models seems to produce surprisingly broad improvements rather than just making them better at the tasks they were explicitly trained for. I'm not sure whether “emergence” is the right explanation, though. Some of it could just be smooth improvements crossing thresholds where abilities become noticeable.
entries.title: scaling improves broadly
entries.summary: Scale improves models beyond their trained tasks; whether that is emergence is left open.

entries.transcript: I think AGI is probably less about reaching some magic level of intelligence and more about being able to reliably transfer what you've learned between very different kinds of problems. An AI system that is brilliant at ten benchmarks but can't generalize outside them doesn't feel generally intelligent to me.
entries.title: AGI is transfer
entries.summary: Generality as reliable transfer between unlike problems rather than a level of intelligence.

entries.transcript: A language model can give a convincing explanation without actually having a stable internal model of the thing it's explaining. Fluency makes it difficult to distinguish genuine understanding from a system that's very good at producing the kind of answer that usually follows a question.
entries.title: fluency without understanding
entries.summary: A convincing explanation does not establish a stable internal model of what is explained.

entries.transcript: I don't think AI alignment is only about preventing catastrophic behavior. Even a system that is extremely capable but consistently optimizes the wrong interpretation of what you meant would be badly aligned. The boring failures seem important because they reveal the same underlying problem at smaller scales.
entries.title: the boring failures
entries.summary: Ordinary misreadings of intent are treated as the same alignment failure at a smaller scale.

entries.transcript: I've started to suspect that intelligence and agency are more separate than I used to think. An AI system could be extremely good at reasoning while having no persistent goals of its own, and I'm not sure whether adding agency actually makes it more intelligent or just more consequential.
entries.title: intelligence without agency
entries.summary: Reasoning and having goals are pulled apart; adding agency may only raise the stakes.

edges.question: If intelligence doesn't require choosing differently, what actually makes a system's reasoning general?
Are retries and indexes examples of the same kind of trade-off, or is that analogy misleading?
If adding complexity can make a system safer, when does simpler is better stop being a useful rule?
How do you decide which information should actually affect a decision?
If increasing capability produces new abilities, how would you distinguish genuine intelligence from a system simply becoming better at many tasks?
If intelligence is different from capability, what would you actually measure to tell the difference?
If a model can display a capability without a stable understanding of what it's doing, what would count as evidence that a new capability reflects genuine understanding?
If general intelligence requires transferring knowledge between domains, does explaining something convincingly without a stable model count as understanding?
Could failures in understanding what a user means be evidence of the same problem as failures in alignment?
If an intelligent system can reason well without having its own goals, where does agency enter the definition of intelligence?
Could a system become better at defending an answer without becoming better at knowing whether the answer is actually right?
You used to think more information generally improves decisions. Does increasing a model's knowledge make its decisions better, or can more information create the same problem?

questions.text: This moves the test from being able to choose otherwise to the decision coming from your own reasoning. What makes the reasoning yours, if it was itself shaped by things you did not choose?
questions.spanQuote: the decision came from our own reasoning

questions.text: The claim is about expected work rather than the time any one lookup takes. What would you measure in a running system to tell a good hash function from a bad one?
questions.spanQuote: the expected work stays roughly constant as the table grows

questions.text: Expertise is given both the tools for noticing an assumption and the tools for defending it. At the time, what would tell you which one you were using?
questions.spanQuote: it can also give you much better ways of defending them

questions.text: The change of mind rests on organisation rather than volume. Does that make the problem the amount of information, or the absence of any way to rank it?
questions.spanQuote: the opposite can happen when the information isn't organized well

questions.text: Capability and intelligence are separated here by what the system decides to do. Is deciding what to do a further capability, or something off that scale entirely?
questions.spanQuote: still be bad at deciding what it should actually be doing

questions.text: Two explanations are offered and neither is taken. What would you have to observe to separate a real discontinuity from a smooth curve crossing a threshold?
questions.spanQuote: smooth improvements crossing thresholds where abilities become noticeable

questions.text: Transfer is made the test in place of raw capability. Across how many unlike problems does a skill have to carry before that counts as general?
questions.spanQuote: reliably transfer what you've learned between very different kinds of problems

questions.text: If fluency and understanding produce the same answer, the difference cannot be read off the answer. Where else would you look for it?
The small failures are read as the large one seen small. What would make a misreading of intent a different failure rather than a smaller one?
questions.spanQuote: they reveal the same underlying problem at smaller scales

questions.text: Reasoning and having goals are pulled apart here. With no goals of its own, what decides which problems the reasoning gets pointed at?
questions.spanQuote: having no persistent goals of its own
